title: What is effective altruism?
html:
What is effective altruism? (8–20 mins)

Effective altruism is the project of using evidence and careful reasoning to work out how to help others as much as possible, and then acting on the answer.

Choose one of these before you continue:

  • Option A: The Definition of Effective Altruism (20 mins). A careful philosophical introduction.

  • Option B: Effective altruism in a nutshell (8 mins, read or listen). A shorter overview.

Why help strangers? (30 mins)

The moral argument behind effective altruism comes from the philosopher Peter Singer. If you walked past a pond and saw a child drowning, you would wade in, even if it ruined your shoes. Singer argues that distance makes no moral difference. If we can prevent something very bad at little cost to ourselves, we should, whether the person is in front of us or in another country.

This idea is called impartiality: everyone’s wellbeing counts equally, wherever they live and whether or not we know them. Many people in this community extend it further, to future generations and to animals. Week 4 asks how far you would extend it.

Read: Peter Singer, The Life You Can Save, chapters 1–2 (free download) (30 mins).

You don’t have to accept the argument. Note where you agree and where you would push back, and bring that to the session.

How we engage with each other

CEA’s guiding principles describe the values this community tries to hold:

  • Commitment to others. We take the wellbeing of others seriously, including distant strangers, future generations and animals.

  • Scientific mindset. We base our actions on evidence and reason, avoid overconfidence and look for critiques of our own views.

  • Openness. We are united by principles, not a specific cause. If the evidence shows a better way of helping, we change course.

  • Integrity. We are honest and trustworthy, and follow rules of good conduct.

  • Collaborative spirit. We treat people with different views, backgrounds and identities with respect.

When EA has fallen short

The community hasn’t always lived up to these principles.

FTX. In 2022 FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange whose founder was closely associated with effective altruism, collapsed. He was later convicted of fraud. Billions of dollars were lost, including money pledged to EA organisations. It raised hard questions about deferring to major donors and missing warning signs. The lessons most people drew are that how you do things matters as much as what you achieve, and that communities need to hold even high-status members to account.

Measurability bias. Early EA focused on interventions whose impact could be counted, such as global health charities. That helped find outstanding giving opportunities, but it neglected problems that are harder to measure, like policy reform and emerging risks. Funders created organisations like Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) to support work that doesn’t fit a cost-effectiveness spreadsheet. Week 3 comes back to this.

Lack of diversity. In the 2024 EA Survey, 69% of respondents were men and 75% were white. People from low- and middle-income countries, where many EA-funded programmes operate, are underrepresented. That narrows the perspectives behind decisions, and it has changed little despite efforts to address it.

Mistakes pages. The Centre for Effective Altruism, 80,000 Hours and GiveWell publish lists of their mistakes. For an outside view, see the criticism section of the Wikipedia article on effective altruism.

Norms for our discussions

  • Be honest about uncertainty. “I’m not sure” is a useful contribution.

  • Understand before you critique. Paraphrase what you heard and ask questions first.

  • Critique ideas, not people.

  • Be willing to change your mind, and say so when someone makes a good point.

  • Assume good faith.
